name: Pinstripe suit

lead:
A pinstripe suit carries narrow, evenly spaced vertical lines in the cloth. Stylists commonly say vertical lines lead the eye along the body and make the wearer look taller and slimmer; this is the reason the pattern appears in advice on dressing to look taller.
The pattern is old: pinstripes were used on suit trousers in the early 19th century and London banks used them to identify employees. Reference sources describe the pattern but do not test its effect on perceived height, so the visual claim rests on style convention.

paras: People wear pinstripe suits as business or formal wear, often in navy or grey, with the stripe thin and closely spaced. Fit and proportion are usually discussed alongside the pattern, as a well-tailored suit shapes the silhouette.
No health risks. Cost depends on cloth and tailoring. Stripes spaced widely or worn on an ill-fitting suit may not give the elongating look people seek.

angle.text: Wearers choose pinstripes for a longer, leaner line from shoulder to hem. It works as an optical effect while the suit is worn, and does not change actual height.

lead: A pinstripe suit is cut from fabric with very thin vertical lines, about 1/30 inch (0.85 mm) wide, often compared with the wider chalk stripe.[1] People who dress to improve their proportions wear it because the vertical lines are said to lengthen the silhouette and make the wearer look taller and leaner.

Pinstripes have appeared on suits since the early 19th century, when London banks used them to identify employees. They were first worn on trousers only and, after US adoption in the 20th century, appeared on jackets too.[1] The pattern is older than suits; Chaucer describes a belt of "pin-stripe stuff" in the Canterbury Tales.[1]
No published study has measured how pinstripes change perceived height; the elongating effect is part of style convention.

paras: Pinstripes first appeared on suit trousers in early 19th-century England and later spread to jackets in the United States.[1]
Style guides say vertical stripes elongate the figure. This is a convention in menswear; the reference sources describe the pattern itself and not perceptual research.[1]
